item.title: Born a Day Too Early?
item.description:
Education

Born a Day Too Early?

Gendered effects of age of school entry on earnings and emotional stability.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Being one of the oldest in class can pay off for women later in life.
  • The same school-age advantage does not appear for men.
  • Women who start school later show greater emotional stability decades later.

This post was co-written with Lisa Hahn.

When a child first steps into a classroom, it feels like a deeply personal milestone. Yet the timing of that step is often determined by administrative rules. Children born just after a school-entry cutoff date must wait an extra year before starting school, while those born just before it enter immediately. As a result, some children begin school as among the oldest in their class, whereas others are among the youngest.

Research suggests that children's early school performance is shaped not only by their age at school entry but also by their relative age, that is, their age compared to their classmates. Older children within a cohort tend to achieve higher grades and perform better on cognitive assessments. However, these advantages generally diminish over time as younger classmates catch up developmentally (Urruticoechea et al., 2021).

The long-term consequences of relative age are less clear. Starting school later delays labor market entry and reduces accumulated work experience. Consistent with this logic, a landmark Swedish study found that later school entry initially lowers earnings, but that this disadvantage is largely offset over the life course (Fredriksson & Öckert, 2014). Hidden behind this average, however, is a striking gender difference: women, as well as individuals from less educated families, tended to earn more during their prime working years when they were among the oldest in their class.

Replicating and extending these findings in Germany, Cygan-Rehm and Westphal (in press) analyzed social security records covering individuals born between 1945 and 1965. For men, being among the oldest rather than the youngest in class had virtually no impact on lifetime earnings. For women, however, entering school later produced a persistent earnings advantage throughout their careers, effectively narrowing the gender pay gap (Cygan-Rehm & Westphal, in press).

Why would a few additional months of age at school entry matter for women's earnings decades later?

The authors examined two possible explanations: delayed childbirth and differential labor market attachment. Women who entered school later became mothers about three months later on average, but they also entered the labor market about three months later. Consequently, they gained no additional years of work before motherhood, nor did school-entry age affect whether they became mothers or how many children they had.

More revealing is what happens around the transition to motherhood. Before their first child is born, women who started school later look virtually identical to those who started earlier in earnings and employment. After childbirth, however, the two groups begin to diverge. Over the following decade, later starters accumulate more employment days and earn more than their peers who entered earlier (Cygan-Rehm & Westphal, in press). The findings suggest that they remain more strongly attached to the labor market precisely when many women's careers experience substantial interruptions.

Could personality be part of the answer?

While these findings identify when the divergence occurs, they tell us little about the psychological processes that might produce it. Why should a difference of only a few months at school entry influence how women navigate one of the most consequential transitions of adult life? A recent study by Barabasch and colleagues (2026) offers an important clue. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) and the National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), the authors examined whether age at school entry is associated with Big Five personality traits in adulthood.

For four of the five traits, the authors found no lasting effects. The sole exception was emotional stability. Women scored almost half a standard deviation lower than men, yet women who entered school as some of the oldest children in their class scored about 0.1 standard deviations higher in adulthood, reducing the gender gap by roughly one-fifth. Men showed no comparable effect, and the advantage persisted from age 25 to 60, appearing strongest around age 45 (Barabasch et al., 2026).

Individuals lower in emotional stability tend to experience more anxiety, worry, and negative affect, making it harder to cope with uncertainty, persevere under stress, or maintain confidence in demanding situations. Higher emotional stability has consistently been linked to higher earnings and better labor market outcomes (Judge et al., 1999; Alderotti et al., 2023).

Taken together, the evidence points to an intriguing pattern. The same arbitrary school-entry cutoff appears to influence both emotional stability and lifetime earnings, and in both cases the effects emerge among women but not men. While no study has yet linked these findings directly, they raise the possibility that personality may be a pathway through which relative age shapes women's later economic outcomes.

How does relative age get under the skin?

Why should being a few months older or younger than classmates leave traces decades later? Barabasch et al. (2026) discuss two possibilities. One focuses on social evaluation. Younger children are routinely compared with older, more mature classmates and may therefore receive more corrective feedback or less favorable evaluations, even when their behavior is age-appropriate. Although achievement differences largely disappear over time (Urruticoechea et al., 2021), these experiences may nevertheless shape how children see themselves. If girls are particularly likely to internalize such evaluations, relative age could gradually become part of their self-concept.

A second possibility focuses more directly on early experiences of competence. Older children often enjoy temporary cognitive, social, and physical advantages. Although these advantages fade as classmates catch up, experiencing oneself as capable or socially effective may have longer-lasting consequences. Small differences in maturity could thus shape children's developing self-confidence and emotional functioning long after the original performance differences have disappeared.

Viewed from this perspective, the most remarkable finding is not that school-entry age predicts women's earnings. It is that developmental differences that largely disappear from view may nevertheless leave lasting traces in personality. Relative age may matter not because it permanently changes what children can do, but because it shapes, however subtly, how they come to see themselves and what they believe they are capable of. What begins as a difference in age relative to classmates may become a difference in how women navigate uncertainty, setbacks, and, decades later, the transition to motherhood itself.

item.title: Should Primary Care Take on a Greater Role in the Care of ADHD?
item.description:
ADHD

Should Primary Care Take on a Greater Role in the Care of ADHD?

Primary care could play a much more important role in ADHD care.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD is not rare, and referral rates have increased across many countries.
  • Most ADHD care has been delivered by specialists, but this is not feasible for such a common condition.
  • All nations need to consider how they shift to a model of care that is accessible and sustainable.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects around 5 percent of children and 2-3 percent of adults.1,2 Although the population level of ADHD has not changed over time, its definition has evolved. Also, public and professional awareness of ADHD has increased. These factors, coupled with historical underrecognition, mean that many countries are witnessing huge increases in referral rates for ADHD assessment and treatment.3,4 This is unsurprising given the greater scientific understanding of ADHD and its risks and the availability of highly effective treatments.5

This increase in ADHD referrals, however, means that where there is publicly funded health care provision, service capacity has not been able to match population need. This has led to deepening inequalities as those who can afford to do so will seek private health care.

Some countries (e.g., Australia) are beginning to shift to greater primary care involvement such that some specialist primary care staff now are trained to take on assessment and treatment. Other countries (e.g., United Kingdom) still rely on specialist care. Given how prevalent ADHD is, an exclusively secondary care, specialist service for ADHD is unsustainable.6 Primary care already plays a leading role in mental health care for common mental health conditions (e.g., anxiety and depression) in many countries. Also, primary care physicians are especially skilled at providing care across the lifespan and in managing physical as well as mental health. So, what are some of the barriers to greater primary care involvement for ADHD?

Key Barriers to Primary Care Involvement in ADHD Diagnosis and Management

A major concern is inadequate funding for primary care to take on a greater role. Also, staff may not be fully trained about ADHD or are left with the responsibility of highly complex individuals and encounter delays in accessing specialist support. This includes those who develop psychiatric comorbidities or are exposed to complex social adversities.

A second concern is that ADHD lies on a dimension, and to make a diagnosis currently requires a lengthy, detailed assessment that would not be feasible typically in routine primary care appointments.

Another concern is that stimulants are first-line medications for ADHD. Whilst highly effective, they are subject to misuse and diversion, which has been the experience in some countries. Guarding against this may be more challenging in primary care.

These challenges are not insurmountable, but they do require political and professional will to change. This includes prioritising funding and training in primary care for an enhanced role. Also, primary and specialist care services need to be well linked and seamless to allow rapid secondary assessment and consultation when needed. Furthermore, primary care needs to include a range of professionals beyond physicians alone (e.g., nurses, pharmacists, and nonpharmacological support such as psychology).

Research Priorities for Optimizing ADHD Care Pathways

Future research needs to examine how best to identify those most suitable for primary versus secondary care. Those with major comorbidities, who are suicidal, exposed to social adversities, or at high familial risk for severe mental illness (e.g., psychosis) are known to have worse outcomes, so they would likely be greater priorities for specialist services.

Other research, some of which is in progress, needs to evaluate the effectiveness of nonstimulants as first- rather than second-line treatment in primary care, as this would reduce risks of diversion in less supervised contexts.

Regardless, across nations, we need to shift our thinking around ADHD as a specialist condition that is rare and move to a model that is more accessible and sustainable but safe.

item.title: Medusa's Mirror: Reflecting the Impact of Trauma
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

Medusa's Mirror: Reflecting the Impact of Trauma

Medusa is often cast as an iconic femme fatale embodying both beauty and danger.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Individuals who have endured trauma often feel disconnected and estranged from their bodies.
  • The myth of Medusa serves as a powerful portal for survivors, resonating on many levels.
  • But a closer read of this story reveals that, to Medusa, her body was no longer hers.

Unresolved trauma can linger in the body long after the threat of harm has passed, rising up as a reaction rather than a memory. For many survivors of trauma, the body is the home of chronic stress, and as a result, it can become a source of pain, shame, and intrusion. In my clinical practice, I have observed that individuals who have endured trauma often feel disconnected and estranged from their bodies.

The myth of Medusa serves as a powerful portal for survivors, resonating on many levels. However, it’s important to recognize that Medusa’s story has often been diminished. Rather than being remembered as a victim of violence, she has been vilified as a dangerous monster to be feared. Her identity was shattered, her community lost, and her dreams of becoming a priestess violently stripped away. Medusa can serve as a mirror by reflecting the impact of trauma on identity, relationships, and the body. Yet for those who resonate with the tragedy of Medusa’s life and death, there is hope. Unlike Medusa, you have the power to reclaim your narrative. Your path can be different; it can be one of healing and transformation.

Medusa’s Story, Stigma, and the Parallel with Modern Trauma Survivors

Medusa is often cast as an iconic femme fatale, embodying both beauty and danger in one mythical creature. But a closer read of this story reveals that to Medusa, her body was no longer hers. Fresh from the carnage of the double assault, Medusa is deeply alone and mourning the loss of the person she was before. Medusa’s humanity is obscured by the label of monster, which others unfairly bestow upon her. In its essence, the story of Medusa is a story of the stigma and shame associated with rape, a heavy burden often carried by the victim rather than the perpetrator in the aftermath of the intrusion trauma. Similar to the plight of many sexual abuse survivors, Medusa endured a private violation followed by repeated incidents of public shaming and alienation.

Even in today’s world, coming forward with claims of sexual harassment and assault is a risky proposition, particularly if the alleged perpetrator is powerful. The #MeToo movement was founded by Tarana Burke to empower survivors of sexual violence and create a platform for individuals to share their experiences. It gained widespread attention in 2017 following several allegations of sexual misconduct against producer Harvey Weinstein, highlighting the prevalence of sexual harassment and assault, particularly in the workplace. Christine Blasey Ford, a professor of psychology, made a retrospective disclosure of abuse in 2018 against U.S. Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, accusing him of sexually assaulting her when they were teenagers. Her testimony during Kavanaugh’s confirmation hearings reignited discussions about sexual assault, consent, and the credibility of survivors’ stories. Ford’s bravery in coming forward with her allegations brought her both support and backlash, highlighting the complexities surrounding issues of sexual assault and the challenges faced by survivors speaking out.

Kyra, a survivor who came to therapy to process the unresolved trauma of sexual abuse, watched the hearings from the sidelines. She explained,

“As I watched Christine Blasey Ford’s testimony and the media coverage of the event, it was so difficult for me as an abuse survivor. Even now as I think about it, tears come to my eyes. The accusations hurled at her and questions as to why she couldn’t remember certain details and why it took her so long to come forward really hit close to home. I believe that only a survivor of sexual abuse can fully understand the shame, the fear, the denial, and the foggy memories that come with such trauma. After so many years of trying to convince myself that it didn’t happen to me, it took me close to thirty-five years before I was finally able to admit my own history of child sexual abuse out loud to another human being and to accept the truth. I understand why the abused don’t come forward. It is because of shame, blame, deep denial, and fear of how others will react.”

Hidden Nature of Sexual Abuse and Its Impact on Connection and Identity

Sexual abuse is not always as explicit and dramatized as the Medusa myth; it is often insidious and concealed by grooming, systematic boundary violations, and broken trust within preexisting close relationships. Many people who have experienced trauma report feeling disconnected and withdrawn from society, finding it difficult to trust or connect with other people again. When understanding the impact of body-based intrusion trauma, it is essential to note the assault it has on a person’s sense of self; survivors often report feeling like “one person before and another person after.” Trauma often involves a loss of self-identity.

Like many survivors of sexual abuse, Medusa experienced a world that became dark and dangerous; she might have come to believe that placing trust in others and forming connections was far more terrifying than enduring a solitary existence. For this reason, the image of Medusa is often used as an emblem for survivors of sexual abuse. Many choose to tattoo her on their bodies as a powerful act of reclamation, honoring her as a survivor rather than a victim. This shared belief allows them to challenge the notion that abuse condemns them to a lifetime of silence, secrecy, and shame. By embracing the Medusa identity, they assert their strength and resilience in the face of trauma.

item.title: The Case for the Case Study
item.description:
Forgiveness

The Case for the Case Study

What statistics, Holocaust descendants and "Fauda" can teach us about individuals.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Variability within groups can reveal important differences that averages conceal.
  • The show "Fauda" illustrates how people can resist assumptions based on identity or group membership.
  • People may share an identity or history while responding to it in profoundly different ways.
  • Outliers can challenge assumptions and sometimes point toward the next scientific discovery.
Difference
Source: RosZie/Pixabay

When I ran a first-ever study at Harvard that brought together descendants of Holocaust survivors and Nazi perpetrators for an organized dialogue, I was struck not only by the statistical findings, but by what the findings made me realize about the relationship between groups and individuals.

I reported the findings in my book Justice Matters: Legacies of the Holocaust and World War II. The study examined how the participants interacted using the statistical method lag sequential analysis to pinpoint average patterns in their verbal exchanges. One finding was that participants on both sides, although in different ways, felt like victims.

I remember discussing the findings with my mentor, Brendan Maher, who reminded me to look carefully at the variability within each group, rather than focusing only on the average statistical findings. Who did not fit the average? What did the outliers look like? Were there qualities that separated people who responded differently? His nudge stayed with me.

Looking for variability

I’ve spent decades teaching research methods, so I knew the importance of variability. But seeing this principle emerge from research involving people having a conversation was eye-opening. When we study human behavior, we often begin with a group. We compare groups, calculate averages, look for statistical patterns, and ask whether differences are meaningful. But there is another question statistics alone cannot answer and that is: What does this finding mean for this particular person?

The average is not the person. A statistical average summarizes a group. It does not describe every individual within that group. The average can tell us what is typical. By contrast, variability can tell us how typical it really is. The problem occurs when a statistical description of a group becomes a prediction about an individual.

Where do I fit within the distribution?

Our histories, experiences, personalities, and choices contribute to who we are. Two people can belong to the same category and still be quite different. The goal is not to dismiss research when it does not correspond to our experience. One person’s experience cannot overturn a well-established finding. However, we need to hold both in mind, including what the research tells us about the group, and how it applies to this individual.

Why the case study matters

A case study allows us to examine an individual in context. So rather than reducing a person to a typical score within a distribution, it lets us examine relationships among experiences, behavior, and meaning over time. A case can also challenge a theory. If most people behave as a theory predicts and one person does not, we might simply label that person an outlier. But the outlier may raise an important question: Why is this person different?

Perhaps there is another variable we have not considered. Perhaps the theory applies only under certain conditions. Perhaps what we thought was one phenomenon consists of several processes. A case does not replace larger-sample research needed to establish causation; rather, a case study shows us how a pattern takes shape in an individual’s life. Whereas statistics can tell us what is typical, a case study can reveal what a pattern leaves unexplained.

Looking again

I think back to the study that brought together descendants of Holocaust survivors and Nazi perpetrators. We found patterns in how participants interacted. But the more interesting question was never just, how did the average participant communicate? It was also, who was different, and why?

For example, among the descendants of Holocaust survivors, there was a striking range of emotional responses to the Holocaust legacy. Some were deeply consumed by the past. The Holocaust remained an emotionally present part of their lives, shaping how they understood themselves and the world around them. For some, this could include an intense desire for justice, and, at times, even revenge.

Others responded very differently. They did not spend much time thinking about their parents’ experiences and were more focused on their present-day identities and lives. The Holocaust was part of their family history, but it did not occupy the same psychological space for all of them.

There was a similar range of emotions among the descendants of Nazi perpetrators. Some felt guilt and responsibility for what their families had done and wanted to acknowledge the past and make amends. Others felt like victims themselves and resisted being held responsible for crimes they had not committed and for which they had not even been alive. They resented being defined by the actions of a previous generation.

These varying responses reveal that sharing a group identity, or even a family history, does not produce a single emotional response. People can inherit the same broad historical past and experience, interpret, and organize that past in remarkably different ways. The statistics helped us see the group pattern, but looking closely at individuals helped us see the variation. Both are needed.

Fauda: Conflicts of the Present

That same principle is relevant to the conflicts of the present. It is tempting, especially during periods of violence, to speak about Jews, Muslims, Christians or any other large category as though each group possessed one mind and one emotional response. But of course, actual people are more varied than the labels suggest.

A contemporary example can be found in the Netflix series Fauda. The series is a fictional drama, not a scientific study of the conflict. But it is psychologically interesting because it repeatedly places individual characters inside categories more nuanced than the categories themselves. For example, the series depicts people from different backgrounds, including Israelis and Palestinians, soldiers and civilians, Muslims, Christians, Bedouins, Druze, and people whose identities cross these usual boundaries. Some characters are committed to violence, and some are motivated by revenge, family, loyalty, or the desire to protect others. Some resist the cycle of violence. In one storyline, a Muslim man tries to save his Israeli Jewish neighbors at a kibbutz.

Whatever one thinks of the show’s politics, these characters complicate the assumption that identity determines behavior. The same complexity was visible to me when I lived in Israel. I encountered Israelis who refused, for reasons of conscience, to participate in the army, and others who believed that past injustices justified war. These differences reflected different understandings of loyalty, responsibility, compassion, and the possibility of peace.

Political, economic, historical, and military factors matter a lot. I’m not suggesting that emotional differences explain a conflict by themselves, or that individual variation erases group histories or unequal power. The narrower psychological point is that within every group, people differ in their capacity for revenge, forgiveness, tolerance for ambiguity, sensitivity to injustice, and ability to imagine the humanity of someone on the other side.

When we ignore that variation, we make people less understandable. We also make reconciliation more difficult, because we assume that everyone in the opposing group is equally committed to the same ends.

The participants in my Holocaust study shared important identities, but they did not respond to the past in identical ways. The characters in Fauda dramatize a similar truth that people inherit histories, but they do not all deal with those histories in the same way.

In sum, whenever we encounter a statistical finding, we can ask two questions: What does this tell us about people in general? And what might it mean for this person? The first keeps us grounded in averages. The second keeps us grounded in individuality.

Percentages, probabilities, and algorithmic predictions can tell us what the average person might do, think, or feel. These numbers can be useful. But they can also create an illusion of certainty. There is a distribution of people. And within that distribution are individuals whose lives are more complicated than any single number can capture. That is why I think we need to bring the case study back into our thinking. Not instead of statistics and group studies but alongside them.

The case study reminds us to look at the person behind the number. When we encounter a finding about a group to which we belong, we can ask: Where do I fit? When we encounter someone from a group we think we understand, we can ask: Who is this person? And when we encounter someone who does not fit the pattern, we can ask the most scientific question of all, which is, why? Sometimes the outlier is simply an outlier. And sometimes the outlier is where a deeper understanding begins.

item.title: The Emotional Lives of Miss USA Winners
item.description:
Beauty

The Emotional Lives of Miss USA Winners

Beauty pageant winners reveal their true feelings.

Posted September 17, 2026

There was a small announcement in the local newspaper that the public was invited to meet with last year’s winners of the Miss USA pageant at the Plaza in downtown Santa Fe, New Mexico. It seemed like an opportunity to see who had been chosen as the icons of beauty.

They were standing around the bandstand, and each one wore a sash that proclaimed the title she had won from each of the 50 states. Viewers were photographing them and asking questions related to fashion, beauty, and modeling. But there was something else I longed to know: did they have any psychological or emotional obstacles that they overcame before winning the accolades?

Hannah Klein, Miss Ohio
Source: Paul Ross, with permission

I started with Miss Ohio, Hannah Klein, wondering if she would be willing to answer my personal questions and was delighted at how open she was. “I was born with heterotaxy, which is a rare birth defect,” she said, “and I was given a 50/50 chance to live past the age of 25. I am 34 now.” She was left with a long scar on the front of her body from extensive surgery and said that the reason she wanted to compete was that she didn’t see a lot of women with scars in the fashion industry.

At her first modeling job, her scar was photoshopped out. “I felt like the normal version of myself and my body were not acceptable. I would never be good enough or beautiful enough. I never heard that a scar was beautiful. I needed other women to see that their own differences didn’t dimmish their worth,” she explained. “Scars don’t need to be filtered or hidden. They are beautiful.” She confided that the most beautiful part of competing was the impact she could have on others and their stories and their mental or physical scars.

Klein wasn’t diagnosed until she was 16, but she knew something wasn’t right. She finally had imaging done and discovered she had five spleens, a heart defect, and other abnormalities, which is what necessitated the surgery that left her with the visible scar. In the world of beauty and fashion photographs, it had to be removed and eliminated. She thought she was okay with that, and on the surface she was. But when she did her first professional swimsuit photos, the photographer left her surgery scar, and she started sobbing. “It healed something in me I didn’t realize was still a bit broken.”

Kelsey Kraft, Miss Alaska
Source: Paul Ross, with permission

Kelsey Craft was Miss Alaska last year. Like Kline, she was forthcoming and willing to talk about her personal life and challenges. Four years ago, she was thrown off a golf cart, landed on her face, and broke her nose and jaw in four places. “I was wired shut for a month,” she said. “I work in aesthetics as an injector in the medical spa industry. Psychologically, when I didn’t know how I would heal, it changed my mindset. Your value isn’t based on how you look and you can lose it at any time. But they can’t take away your heart and the way you treat people or the way you show up in the world with kindness.”

Craft was named Miss International in 2017, in one of the world’s most prestigious beauty pageants. But did she always feel beautiful? She revealed that she grew up tall, and only when she got into pageants did she think that her height could be an advantage. “I wasn’t asked to dance because I was taller than all the boys at 5’11”. I grew up lower middle class with a single mom. We didn’t have money to buy school clothes every year. My jeans were never long enough. I was nicknamed Highwater Girl, and I still feel my clothes aren’t long enough.”

When asked how she felt about giving beauty injections to clients, she replied: “Who am I to judge what makes a woman feel more confident?”

Issha Mata, Miss Hawaii
Source: Paul Ross, with permission

Issha Mata was selected as Miss Hawaii last year. She said that her journey before that was difficult. She never placed before she won, and only got as far as the semi-finals. She never felt good enough. She thought she was “too Hawaiian.” “In California, I wasn’t Californian enough. In the Philippines, I wasn’t Filipino enough. Going back to Hawaii was my chance and my choice to really represent the culture and the people. It wasn’t just about residency and where you live.”

On the Big Island, she went to an all-Hawaiian school, with the teaching in Hawaiian and English. Only one percent of the people speak Hawaiian. “Everything was Americanized when we were colonized by the U.S.,” she explained. “I feel hurt but we can’t go back and fix what happened to us; we can go forward and represent our culture in authentic ways. When I competed at Miss USA my costume was not glitz and glam like the others. It was tapa cloth and I was barefoot. Everyone wore heels and glitter and I was barefoot in cloth. Walking onto the stage, I did a chant called Kunihi ka mauna — a welcome chant. It talks about my island, the Big Island.”

Mata said that she represented a chiefess named Manono who joined a battle to preserve the kapu system of traditional Hawaiian values. She is 5’6” tall, and said that it was hard for her to see the other girls in glam when she was short and “not looking USA enough. But I wanted to represent the culture and the nation and not just my state.” To her surprise and amazement, she won.

For 75 years, the Miss USA organization says that it has showcased the dynamic, accomplished women who reflect the confidence, diversity, and ambition of modern America. The USA national title holders shape beauty, culture and conversation, they claim.

Source: Paul Ross, with permission

I would add that the three women said that they were grateful that they got to talk about themselves emotionally and psychologically and not just about fashion, beauty, modeling, and clothes.

item.title: Wild Flourishing: Should Animals Have Territorial Rights?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Wild Flourishing: Should Animals Have Territorial Rights?

Pablo Castello considers how animals feel when they lose their homes.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Mule deer and other animals inherit knowledge across generations where they live that is vital for survival.
  • Castello argues that wild animals should have rights to reside in their territories.
  • Granting agency would honor wild flourishing—the opinions of wild animals—and advance interspecies justice.
Source: Nicky Pe / Pexels

Philosophers, legal scholars, and people interested in the growing, diverse field of animal studies often ponder alluring, important, and rather difficult questions. Some of these queries involve whether or not wild animals should be granted the right to own their homes, or whether they are merely renters, and whether we should try to reduce the suffering of wild animals, and where we should draw the line and let things be, no matter how horrific they are.

Along these lines, another important question arises that centers on the territory/residency rights of wild animals and what they may be. This is among the reasons why I was very interested in an essay titled "The Territorial Rights of Wild Animals: Justification" by Pablo P. Castello. Focusing on mule deer—but his discussion is relevant to other nonhumans—he argues that deer do not simply inhabit landscapes and that their ability to lead social and cultural lives that they have control over depends on residing in their territories or homes.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write "The Territorial Rights of Wild Animals: Justification" and how does it relate to your areas of interest?

Pablo P. Castello: I wrote it for a number of reasons, including these two. First, because in areas such as wildlife management, animals are often treated as a nuisance or a function of their ecological role, overlooking that their lives matter in their own right. The literature on territorial rights is very rich and helps demonstrate why animals’ ties to particular territories matter so deeply that they place duties on humans to recognize and respect their rights.

Second, because in territorial rights scholarship, most authors treat animals as mere resources, akin to minerals. Instead of conceiving of wild animals as resources, I wanted to send a simple message to territorial rights experts: “If you agree with the nuanced arguments made by some of the field’s leading authors, you should also agree that some wild animals should have territorial rights.”

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

PPC: I hope the article will interest territorial rights, animal rights, and conservation scholars, as well as wildlife advocates, managers, and policymakers beyond academia.

MB: What are some of your major messages, and why would the general public be interested in your research?

PPC: A significant portion of the public is concerned about the future of wild animals. UNESCO’s “World in 2030” Public Survey, which gathered responses from more than 15,000 people worldwide, found that climate change and biodiversity loss were by far the most frequently identified challenges facing peaceful societies over the coming decade, chosen by 67 percent of respondents.

“The Territorial Rights of Wild Animals” speaks to this concern by offering new reasons for recognizing wild animals and their communities as right-bearers—rights that would help prevent biodiversity loss.

There are two key messages. The first concerns what I call the “rich lives of animals” and why they matter. The article makes visible the depth and breadth of animals’ social, cultural, and political lives, showing that wild animal communities—specifically, mule deer communities—often have intergenerational cultures anchored in specific places. They also make their own decisions and organize their own social life.

The ethnographic evidence I analyze suggests that we should understand some wild animal communities as animal nations whose cultures, identities, and forms of social organization are so tied to their territories, and so morally and politically important, that they place duties on us humans to respect their territorial rights.

The second message is more practical. U.S. state governments and governments around the world routinely treat nonhuman animals as resources to be counted, managed, controlled, and, when deemed convenient, killed. Terms such as “populations,” “ecosystem services,” “ecosystem integrity,” and even “biodiversity” frequently obscure that animals are individuals and members of social communities with relationships, knowledge, traditions, and homes of their own.

Yet policymakers continue to permit killing animals for recreational purposes through hunting. They fail to build enough wildlife crossings and allow development to fragment, and sometimes even destroy, the territories on which wild animal peoples depend.

My article offers new reasons for pursuing different policies: prohibiting recreational hunting, placing stronger limits on development in wild animal territories, and protecting animals’ ability to remain in their homes, migrate through familiar landscapes, and raise their young in the places their communities have relied on for generations.

MB: How does your work differ from those who have similar interest?

PPC: It differs in at least two important ways. First, territorial rights scholars address the “particularity” question: Why should a given people, state, or nation have a moral right to a particular territory? Yet virtually all territorial rights theorists treat animals as resources. My article argues that this is internally inconsistent because the arguments these theorists use to justify human territorial rights also apply to some wild animals.

Second, some of my animal rights colleagues, including Josh Milburn, Steve Cooke, and John Hadley, have developed nuanced arguments for justifying why wild animals should have property rights. I agree that wild animals should have rights to inhabit certain territories because their habitats provide the goods—such as food—they need to meet their basic needs. My article shares this starting point but goes further in two respects.

One is that it grounds animals’ territorial rights not only in basic needs but also in the social dimensions of their lives and the attachment of their collective identities to particular territories. For example, a mule deer's ability to grieve relatives and close friends depends on the safety provided by their knowledge of and familiarity with the territories to which they belong.

The other concerns control. Whereas property rights scholars understand control rights as protecting access to and use of resources, I argue that mule deer, as individuals and nations, should also have territorial rights because those rights would enable them to shape their own futures. Many aspects of their social lives depend on decisions made in specific territories. For example, elder members of mule deer communities teach fawns their community-specific cultures and social norms within intergenerational calving grounds, where familiarity with and knowledge of their territory create the sense of safety that enables this learning.

MB: Are you hopeful that your work will be beneficial to animals so that they will not be viewed as mere resources?

PPC: I am. Many people are motivated by hope—by the belief that change, however difficult, will eventually be achieved. But given climate change, the likely rise of dangerous forms of artificial intelligence, and the likelihood that conditions for us and other animals will significantly worsen, I think we need reasons to do what’s right regardless of hope.

item.title: ChatGPT Health: Solution or Experiment?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

ChatGPT Health: Solution or Experiment?

Has OpenAI put a chatbot in the driver’s seat before it has passed its test?

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • OpenAI recently rolled out ChatGPT Health despite poor evidence of efficacy.
  • Disclaimers and caveats are likely to fall on deaf ears.
  • Industry leaders continue to call for greater restraint; but it may be too late for public health.

More than 300 million people consult ChatGPT for health-related questions every week. To accommodate the demand, OpenAI quietly rolled out ChatGPT Health last month to a select group of US adults; a soft opening of sorts. For the world’s first patient-focused AI, there was surprisingly little fanfare, and I can’t help but think there was a reason.

ChatGPT Health is based on the same underlying architecture as regular ChatGPT, but with a key difference: with permission, the AI can link to your medical records and download health metrics recorded by Apple wearables, such as the Apple Watch. Though initially a separate tab in ChatGPT’s interface, it’s now seamlessly integrated; an operational decision by OpenAI after seeing users posing health questions to the chatbot organically during daily conversations. An OpenAI press release said ChatGPT Health can “help explain a visit note, understand lab results, dig into doctor-patient discussions, and help prepare questions for follow-up appointments…” The platform can optimize the user’s experience with more “personalized conversations.”

But this initiative has tension at its heart. On the one hand, OpenAI qualifies the rollout by saying it’s not for diagnosis or treatment and is “not designed to replace the care and judgment of qualified medical professionals.” On the other hand, that’s exactly what the public will use it for, and OpenAI knows it. "The reality is, we're living in a time when not everyone has access to quality care or care in a timely manner,” said one executive to reporters last month. “The average doctor appointment in the United States is less than 15 minutes... You're often left on your own to sort through a lot of fragmented information.” For many, the black box that is ChatGPT Health will be used in the absence of a physician; after all, if users had access to their doctor, what would they need from AI?

A Limited Skillset

When ChatGPT launched in 2022, it operated exclusively on its “parametric” architecture; that is, it was entirely constrained by the reams of text-based data on which it had been trained, hence the name Large Language Model (LLM). A query such as “What’s the best source of vitamin C?” would prompt the AI to draw on the statistical model it developed during training to predict the most likely word sequence in a response. The model’s strength was its conversation mimicry: fluent, confident, and generally articulate. The weakness was that the training data were scattered, comprising everything from open-access research papers and mainstream articles to blog posts, Q&A forums (e.g., Reddit), and even social media—a cesspit of misinformation. A user asking about vitamin C would need to hope that “guava, kiwi, and citrus fruit” appeared more often in the training data than “sausages and caviar.” Worse still, if the query wasn’t covered in training, the AI would fabricate an answer, like a teenager trying to impress his friends. The hallucination was born.

But AI is evolving at a pace that makes our own evolutionary history appear positively glacial. In the spring of 2023, ChatGPT was upgraded with its RAG plugin, short for retrieval-augmented generation. This software bolt-on lets current AI generations perform online searches in real-time when the AI deems its training data insufficient for a full-throated reply. And while this hands AI the keys to the full wealth of human digital knowledge, there’s a wrinkle: finding data isn’t the same as evaluating it. You can give someone access to the entire PubMed catalog, but it doesn’t mean they’ll be able to make clinical decisions. So, for AI and humans alike, access to information isn’t the limiting factor; rather, it’s the ability to distinguish among quality sources, weigh evidence, and apply knowledge and experience. These are qualities AI doesn’t possess.

The Shallow Body of Evidence

Programming an AI with these high-level skills is certainly possible, but it’s proving complex. And published audits on health-related content suggest better AI reasoning will be crucial to the success of initiatives like ChatGPT Health.

One recent study found that chatbots given medical queries produced “problematic” responses one-fifth to one-half of the time, and “unsafe” responses varied from 5 to 13% of the total. Our own audit of five AI chatbots, published earlier this year in the British Medical Journal, recorded “problematic” answers in roughly 50% of chatbot responses to health questions in misinformation-prone fields; one-fifth were expert-rated as “highly problematic,” and could potentially cause harm if followed. These are two among dozens of studies on the efficacy of AI health-related outputs, showing them to be inconsistent and unreliable.

The limited data on ChatGPT Health, in particular, is no less disconcerting. In a structured test of triage recommendations, Ramaswamy and colleagues at Mount Sinai Health System, NY, reported that 52% of gold-standard emergencies were under-triaged, directing patients with diabetic ketoacidosis or impending respiratory failure to 24–48 h evaluation rather than the emergency department. A preprint awaiting peer review similarly indicates that ChatGPT Health agrees with nurse and physician triage decisions only 50% of the time.

A 50% under-triage rate for genuine emergencies is not a marginal performance defect; it has major implications with asymmetric consequences: over-triage a minor ailment risks stressing a medical system already near breaking point, but under-triaging a real emergency can be catastrophic. The evidence suggests AI is not a suitable tool for first-contact triage. Try telling that to the >40 million people who turn to ChatGPT with healthcare questions every day.

***

None of this means that lower-risk functions are unsafe. For example, the AI may accurately translate clinical terminology, organize medical records, plot and analyze lab results chronologically, and help users prepare questions for their clinician. The difficulty is that ChatGPT Health does not maintain a dependable boundary between those functions and clinical judgment; the moment it interprets symptoms and offers advice, it becomes a functioning triage system, irrespective of OpenAI’s disclaimer. There’s a mismatch between what the system is designed to do and how the end user will ultimately use it. And there’s no evidence that the AI itself understands that limitation.

The good news is that OpenAI continues to evaluate ChatGPT Health using an assessment matrix it developed called Health Bench. Created in collaboration with 262 physicians from 60 countries, across 26 medical specialties, Health Bench periodically audits thousands of conversations to identify and repair weaknesses in the platform. It’s a robust and necessary step, but no data have been published yet, and it’s clearly a work in progress rather than a finished product.

Such public-facing initiatives continue even as industry leaders call for greater restraint. In September 2026, OpenAI’s Sam Altman joined Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and Elon Musk in calling for a slowdown in advanced AI development, with stronger safeguards and independent oversight. The same principle applies to healthcare: safety checks must keep pace with capability. That isn’t happening.

Consider the consequences if Ford rolled out a new truck before proving it was safe to drive. We wouldn’t accept a half-baked product or the manufacturer’s reassurance that it was a “work in progress.” We should demand the same accountability from companies with so much potential influence on public health. Without that accountability, we are the last phase of the experiment.

item.title: Is Philosophy Dead?
item.description:
Philosophy

Is Philosophy Dead?

The fate of philosophy in a scientific age.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • "Scientific philosophy" seeks to closely align philosophical inquiry with scientific methods.
  • Traditional, nonscientific philosophy is increasingly seen as outdated or even "dead."
  • Many leading philosophical minds now work in scientific fields outside philosophy departments.
Will Science Replace Philosophy?
Source: AI-generated with Chat-GPT / OpenAI

Will science replace philosophy?

“Philosophy is under attack.”

If one hears that sentence in today’s discussions, it largely refers to the repeated (and often successful) attempts to close philosophy departments, especially in the United Kingdom and the United States.

But not too long ago, such sentences would have largely been heard in the context of the rapid advances of the sciences. If we look at the history of the sciences, we can see the gradual emancipation of fields of inquiry once seen as part of philosophy develop a degree of independence. What was once called natural philosophy or experimental philosophy became science. And so it was only natural to speculate that philosophy, as a whole, may one day be replaced.

Take this excerpt from Stephen Hawking and Leonard Mlodinow’s The Grand Design:

We each exist for but a short time, and in that time explore but a small part of the whole universe. But humans are a curious species. We wonder, we seek answers. Living in this vast world that is by turns kind and cruel, and gazing at the immense heavens above, people have always asked a multitude of questions: How can we understand the world in which we find ourselves? How does the universe behave? What is the nature of reality? Where did all this come from? Did the universe need a creator? Most of us do not spend most of our time worrying about these questions, but almost all of us worry about them some of the time.

Traditionally these are questions for philosophy, but philosophy is dead. Philosophy has not kept up with modern developments in science, particularly physics. Scientists have become the bearers of the torch of discovery in our quest for knowledge.

Naturalist philosophers, like Daniel Dennett, were quick to counter these kinds of statements. People like me and many other scientifically minded philosophers don’t believe that philosophy has truly died.

And yet, if we look at philosophy as a whole, the naturalist philosopher, or I should rather say "scientific philosopher," really is much closer to Hawking and many other scientists who have become skeptical about the value of philosophy than their defenses let on. Consider the following quote from Hans Reichenbach’s The Rise of Scientific Philosophy:

The scientific philosopher is not afraid of such antagonism. He leaves it to the old-style philosopher to invent philosophical systems, for which there still may be a place assignable in the philosophical museum called the history of philosophy—and goes to work.

Reichenbach and the logical empiricists at large really did think like Hawking that the philosophy of the past was pretty much dead. But from its ashes rises a new philosophy:

Scientific philosophy.

Reichenbach planned to create a new journal with other scientific philosophers like Carnap and Quine, but he unfortunately died in 1953.

To many analytic philosophers, naturalism is seen as the default position in the field, and yet the work of philosophers that is truly continuous with the sciences, deeply engaged with the methods and results of the sciences, is frequently derided as not really being philosophy, such as the psychological studies of experimental philosophers. The return of intuitionist methods, rationalist metaphysics, and the like is claimed to now be in harmony with naturalism. But it is not.

Philosophy today is marked by an uneasy peace between two entirely different ways of doing philosophy— namely, scientific philosophy and unscientific philosophy.

The scientific philosopher sees philosophy as a field sitting between the department buildings of the other sciences. It is part of the sciences. The unscientific philosopher claims privileged access to unique philosophical methods and a stark demarcation between science and philosophy and is at home in the humanities. For they reject the view that philosophy is science—the most abstract science of all.

Of course, very few philosophers would adopt the label of “unscientific” for themselves. Naturally, most philosophers think that they are drawing on the sciences in just the right way and to a sufficient extent to address the philosophical questions they are interested in. But that does not mean they actually are.

The scientific philosophy naturalists like Dennett dreamed of was one in which philosophy operates much like the sciences, collaborating extensively with scientists and blurring the imagined boundaries between science and philosophy. Unfortunately, this is largely prevented by our institutional structures. For philosophers to seriously start working in interdisciplinary teams, they’d have to wait until they are tenured, for such work is still seen with suspicion in the field, even though philosophy is alleged to have undergone a “naturalist turn” in the last century. Some of the best philosophers today aren’t professional philosophers at all. They sit in other departments, such as neuroscience, biology, economics, and physics. For it is becoming increasingly difficult to do good work in philosophy without an in-depth acquaintance with the sciences.

Hawking and other scientists are ultimately right.

Philosophy, as it is commonly understood, is dead.

Science dealt a death blow to a vision of philosophy that is dominant among the public and common among philosophers: a philosophy that is separate from the sciences. Unscientific philosophy, for the radical naturalist, must appear as pseudo-philosophy. It no longer meets scholarly standards for the pursuit of objective truth.

Naturalist philosophy in the sense of truly scientific philosophy, however, is alive and well. It is part of science itself. And it’s what Stephen Hawking and Leonard Mlodinow themselves engaged in when they wrote The Grand Design. But it's up to the philosophy profession to make sure that we engage in it with much closer proximity to the sciences than we have done so far. Otherwise, it will simply be reborn within the sciences themselves.

item.title: Innovation Is Sex
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Innovation Is Sex

What can Esther Perel's work teach us about our organizations?

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Just as desire needs mystery, organizational innovation requires novelty rather than complete predictability.
  • Designing purely for efficiency calcifies culture, rendering it rigid and uninspiring.
  • Intentionally introducing friction can reintroduce the unpredictability required for genuine breakthroughs.

Esther Perel is having a moment.

She consulted on Olivia Wilde and Seth Rogen’s film, "The Invite"; Apple TV just recruited her to host its first-ever dating show, "The Last Person on Earth"; and she’s about to launch a new live show in December called "Strangers, Friends, and Lovers: A Night Out With Esther Perel." Oh, and by the way, it’s the 20th anniversary of her landmark bestselling book Mating in Captivity. Safe to say she's on to something we’re interested in.

When Mating in Captivity came out, the well-trod belief about couples was that emotional closeness leads to a better sex life. But in her book, she lays out the argument for why that’s not quite the case. Yes, emotional closeness is good for relationships; it breeds stability and intimacy (pun intended), but it doesn’t exactly stoke the flame of desire. Desire is fueled by novelty, and novelty requires mystery and intrigue, even uncertainty. As Perel puts it:

“Love enjoys knowing everything about you; desire needs mystery. Love likes to shrink the distance that exists between me and you, while desire is energized by it. If intimacy grows through repetition and familiarity, eroticism is numbed by repetition. It thrives on the mysterious, the novel, and the unexpected.”

This creates something of a paradox in our relationships. If the goal is to have stability and strong emotional bonds and also to have strong desire and sex, what are we to do?

Wait, What Does This Have to Do With Work?

What is of particular interest in seeing Perel’s work continue to spread into mainstream culture is how generalizable her insights seem to be. The relationship patterns she describes show up constantly in our daily lives and in our workplaces, albeit in less romantic ways.

We design teams and organizations to be as stable and predictable as possible, and then we’re surprised when they begin to feel inflexible and stale. We strive to create frictionless systems that help us be maximally productive, then struggle to pinpoint why our work feels uninspired. The tensions that develop when we over-rotate on stability and predictability are similar to those that we might describe in a relationship.

Just as relationships are shaped by routines, the patterns of behavior a group relies on as it solves problems together define organizational culture (Schein and Schein, 2017). Early-stage companies typically contend with massive amounts of uncertainty as they figure out their product/service and how to deliver it to a market. Because of this, they also tend to be exciting, innovative environments. Success at the early stage means learning how to deliver a product/service at scale, which requires systems and processes. Over time, the routines that allow for consistent delivery—that make for stable relationships—are the same ones that cause things to ossify.

The Problem Isn't Just Systems and Routines

The tensions that exist between our desire for stability and creativity are relevant to how we think about organizational culture and change, but there's a deeper dynamic at play here that can't be ignored: trust. And when we're talking about trust, we're talking about risk and uncertainty. As Rachel Botsman defines it, trust is "a confident relationship with the unknown." The trust that lets two people risk being vulnerable with each other has a direct analogue in the psychological safety that lets a team member risk saying a bad idea out loud.

And yet, just as a couple can have plenty of trust and zero desire, an organization can have plenty of psychological safety and zero innovation. Trust is necessary, but not sufficient, for relationships and organizations alike.

In fact, watch what happens when I make a simple translation of that earlier quote into organizational language:

Organizations enjoy knowing everything about their operations; innovation needs mystery. Organizations like to shrink the distance that exists between ideas and execution, while innovation is energized by it. If organizations improve through repetition and familiarity, innovation is numbed by repetition. It thrives on the mysterious, the novel, and the unexpected.

Perel obviously didn't design Mating in Captivity as a management book, but 20 years on, it sure can read like one anyway. The patterns she noticed in bedrooms can just as well describe boardrooms and product teams.

It is no coincidence, then, to learn where Perel's thinking seems to be headed next. At TED this year, in a session called Relational Metamorphosis, she built her breakout around a proposition that should sound familiar by now: Friction, the thing we spend most of our energy avoiding, is actually the raw material for transformation, both personal and collective. She's making the same argument at a societal scale that she made about desire at the relational level 20 years ago. We've gotten so good at engineering the friction out of our lives that we've engineered away the conditions that let anything new happen.

So what do you do with an organization that's become too efficient to innovate?

  • Create some good friction (Blankenship and Sass, 2026). You might re-evaluate a recent process that you've automated and map out the potential downsides of the automation. Don't assume that adding artificial intelligence (AI) to every process will necessarily improve it. Aside from the need to preserve some amount of human judgment and relational attunement in our organizations, the spread of AI demotivates employees.
  • You might block time for thinking that has no discernible ROI. Schedule unstructured time as part of your work. Call it "writing time" if you need to, but take Jerry Seinfeld's advice: During that time you don't have to write, but you can't do anything else. Let a team meet just to communicate; let them sit with a half-formed idea. Increase the distance between ideas and execution.
  • Allow for unpredictable collisions among people instead of routing every interaction through a meeting or a process. Let people play and explore new ideas.

Here's the secret: None of these ideas will solve the problem. But here's another secret: That's the point. This kind of problem is not exactly solvable; it's the kind of dynamic that you tinker and experiment with. It requires trying something new, seeing what happens, reflecting on it, and then trying something else. This can be quite uncomfortable; we're trafficking in uncertainty, after all, but it's always when we least expect it that something new comes crashing in.

item.title: From Research Subject to Research Partner
item.description:
Motivation

From Research Subject to Research Partner

How patient engagement can change more than science.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Patient involvement and engagement in research can benefit patients, not just research.
  • Research involvement can build confidence and community and restore a sense of purpose and agency.
  • Patient involvement must be meaningful, voluntary, and supported.

Emma Collins, Patient and Public Involvement Manager, Encephalitis International

Source: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels

Much that is written about patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) focuses on how the involvement of patients and their caregivers improves research. Lesser attention is given to the equally important question: What does participating in research do for the patient?

Through the words of those affected by neurological illness and brain injury who have since engaged with research, this post will challenge the assumption that PPIE is carried out only to benefit research and researchers. Rather, it will show that PPIE can become an aspect of a person’s recovery and reintegration into society following a brain injury.

When I realized that speaking was triggering partial paralysis/seizures to my face, I avoided speaking… After each episode, I could feel my cognitive abilities, vision and motor skills failing. As I remained silent, I made a promise to myself. If and when I speak again, I will advocate for research and use my voice for good—to help others learn more about this condition. That's my motivation, my promise to myself when I didn't speak. –A woman affected by LGI1 encephalitis in Canada

Research involvement activities do not just contribute to medical knowledge; although PPIE will not provide a cure or be able to give answers that the patient or their family members may have, it can help people to rebuild an understanding of themselves and their "new normal."

PPIE can provide a way to restore a sense of agency, giving the opportunity to share experience and, in doing so, improve the experiences and outcomes of the next person to be given a serious illness or brain injury diagnosis.

… Any new treatments are probably way too late for us, but if it helps somebody else to be diagnosed more quickly, then I’m all for it… I have a lot of knowledge, which I would like to use to help other people... I’ve lost my husband and the life we used to share …We have both said that helping to educate other sufferers and raise awareness within the medical world too would be a great achievement. –A caregiver and spouse of a person affected by LGI1 encephalitis in the United Kingdom, reflecting on what lead them to support research

The achievement of taking part in and contributing to research can help patients to build confidence in themselves and their ability to make a positive influence on future medical knowledge and understanding.

…I had to re-learn how to read, write and speak. Being able to participate in a formal research event feels like an achievement; it’s a boost to my confidence. In the first year I was diagnosed with encephalitis, being an independent woman seemed like an almost unachievable goal, as I relied on the support of other family members doing the most simple everyday tasks...The fact that I have now been able to do these tasks whilst participating in the studies of a variety of wonderful researchers still feels like a little miracle …Most importantly of all, it makes me feel that my experience of recovery is really valued by professional experts… Research is vital. –A woman affected by HSV1 encephalitis in the United Kingdom, reflecting on what motivated her to get involved in research and what she has personally gained from doing so

Taking part in patient involvement and research activities can ensure that purpose is gained from the illness. Those who experience a serious illness or injury often hope that no one will have to go through what they did, and engaging with research is a way of honouring that hope.

…My motivation is primarily this.… if awareness of this is built and spread, it could help someone in quicker diagnosis and perhaps could help someone carry a lesser emotional burden…Particularly in a country like India, where the awareness of such illnesses is almost zero, such studies could become a guiding light... –A man affected by NMDAR encephalitis in India, reflecting on what he feels the benefits are of supporting research

Engaging with PPIE sessions fosters community, building a sense of belonging by bringing together people with a shared purpose and understanding of the possible impacts of their respective illness or injury.

…I highly recommend patients and care givers to support researchers. That way we are building a community to stand with each other and support each other navigating hard times. Encephalitis is a hard disease, and the journey is often difficult. This global community can support peers and care givers not just with information but also with support on how to deal with this tough journey. –A woman affected by CASPR2 encephalitis from India, sharing her experience of contributing to research and why she would encourage others to join her in doing so

It is important to recognise that PPIE may not be appropriate for everyone. Therefore, PPIE should always be voluntary, supported, flexible, and appropriately reimbursed (where research funding allows), and there should be a consideration of potential emotional harm unintentionally arising from PPIE. Lived experience should never be exploited in the name of advancing research.

So, as well as asking: "How can patients improve our research?" researchers could also ask: "How can our research improve the lives of the patients who help us?" The testimonies shared demonstrate the value in PPIE, making a clear call to action for researchers to utilise as many opportunities as possible to include patients and caregivers—not only to improve research design or research outcomes but also to remind people that there is power in their lived experience, power that they can harness to support their recovery journey.

My most sincere and grateful thanks to members of the Encephalitis International community for their contribution to this blog post and to encephalitis research worldwide.

item.title: Bonding with Someone Rebounding from Romantic Rejection
item.description:
Mating

Bonding with Someone Rebounding from Romantic Rejection

When suddenly single, attention and acceptance facilitate attraction.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Romantic rejectees exhibit a high amount of prosocial behavior toward new dating partners.
  • Rejected partners do not behave more aggressively toward prospective paramours.
  • Most people are able to mate switch: evaluate alternative partners post break-up.

Many singles have acquaintances they would have considered potential romantic prospects if they were available. If this acquaintance suddenly becomes single, the question becomes what approach is appropriate under the circumstances. Fortunately, research shows the path forward doesn't have to be awkward; it can instead be respectful, approachable, and authentic.

Source: Image by Hans from Pixabay

Smitten With the Suddenly Single

There are a variety of opinions regarding the state of mind of the suddenly single, usually based on the circumstances of their recent breakup. We don’t characterize such people as “available,” because we usually see that they aren't ready to dash back onto the dating scene. Some people even characterize a new romance as a “rebound,” even without evidence to support that assumption. From the rejectee's perspective, however, things often look very different.

Post-Breakup Prosocial Behavior

Dongming Qin and team (2026) explored how newly single partners behave after suffering romantic rejection in a piece entitled “Moving on Gracefully.”[i] Their study consisted of 150 participants between the ages of 17 and 26, 99 women and 51 men, aged 17 to 26 years. They measured romantic consideration through the lens of possibility of acceptance (PA), the prospect of being accepted by others, a perception that can influence the rejectees' behavioral response.

Qin and team studied how rejectees behaved toward a new dating partner who displayed high versus low levels of PA. They noted that rejectees exhibited more prosocial behavior toward new dating partners compared with individuals who had not been rejected. They further found that rejectees showed a higher level of prosocial behavior toward a new dating partner who had a high PA compared to those with lower levels of PA.

However, contrary to their expectations, they also found that rejectees were not more aggressive toward new dating partners than non-rejected individuals, and did not exhibit more aggression toward new partners with low PA than those with high PA.

Qin and team suggest that romantic rejectees were more prosocial than aggressive toward new dating partners compared with non-rejected individuals, indicating that romantic rejection motivates the adoption of prosocial behavior as a strategy to regain a sense of acceptance. They note this is consistent with the social reconnection hypothesis, which posits that social rejection prompts affiliative behavior toward new people. Rejectees project a willingness to reconnect with new prospective paramours, which can facilitate disengagement from ex-partners and soothe the sting of past romantic rejection.

Qin and team also note their results are consistent with the mate-switching hypothesis: that people may evaluate alternative partners and manage transitions between relationships. Viewed from this perspective, prosocial behavior may facilitate social reconnection and provide a strategy for new romantic opportunities post-breakup.

Proceed With Caution

When spending time with a newly single romantic prospect, research shows the value in taking things slowly. Expressing genuine interest, attention, and compassion not only signals high PA, but it also provides rejectees a safe space to discuss their recent breakup if they choose. Forming new relationships within this comfortable social environment also decreases the likelihood of a “rebound,” promoting resilience instead and creating a relationship based on respect, authenticity, and love.
